ig_tt_text:
This scratch ticket tells you if it's a winner before you even scratch it.

In 2003 Toronto geological statistician Mohan Srivastava noticed that the printed numbers on a tic-tac-toe scratch game gave the winners away: numbers that appeared only once ("singletons") lining up three in a row meant a winner about 9 times out of 10. He didn't cash in — he called the lottery, and the game was pulled the next day.

Sources: WIRED (2011), AP/Fox News (2011). Reconstruction, Canadian case.

yt_desc:
In 2003 Mohan Srivastava, a geological statistician in Toronto, found a flaw in a tic-tac-toe scratch lottery game: the visible numbers revealed the winners. Numbers printed only once on the ticket (singletons) that formed a row of three predicted a winning ticket about 90% of the time. Instead of exploiting it, he reported it to the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation, which pulled the game the next day.

Sources:
- WIRED, 'Cracking the Scratch Lottery Code' (Jan 31, 2011)
- AP / Fox News, 'Statistician cracks secret code behind lottery tickets' (Feb 2, 2011)
